lesson_title: Two Pages and a Spine: Triangle Rules in 2D and 3D
hook_text: A fence you cannot walk to, measured from the dry corner — and a 3D mast problem that is secretly two flat triangles.
clip_script: A farmer owns a triangular field. Two fences leave the same corner post: one runs 6 units, the other 11, opening at 50 degrees. The third boundary crosses a marsh nobody can wade. How long is that unreachable fence? The hinge tool: the far side squared equals 6 squared plus 11 squared, minus 2 times 6 times 11 times cos 50. That is 157 minus about 85 — roughly 72 — square root, 8,49 units. And watch the correction term, because it is the whole idea. At exactly 90 degrees the cosine dies and the rule shrinks to Pythagoras. Pinch the corner tighter and the far side shortens. Open it past 90 and the cosine goes negative, the correction adds, the fence stretches. Pythagoras with a hinge. Then the 3D secret: a mast problem is never really 3D — it is two flat triangles like pages of an open book, sharing one spine. Solve the page holding the data, carry the spine's length to the standing page, multiply by tan of the elevation, and the height falls out. Find the pair, find the hinge, find the spine.
visual_style: A drone shot over a triangular field with a shimmering marsh, fence lines drawing themselves from the dry corner, then the scene folding upright into two book pages joined at a glowing spine beside a radio mast.
pacing: Steady build through the fence numbers, a snap on the Pythagoras-with-a-hinge line, smooth fold into the two-page finale.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and crack any triangle, flat or standing.
